summary:
Police conduct is the clearest documented danger. In September 2017 national police in Baku detained at least 100 members of the LGBT community in raids conducted ostensibly against prostitution; dozens were held on dubious charges, at least 60 people were imprisoned or fined, and beatings, forced medical examinations, interrogation, blackmail, threats of rape and the use of electric shocks were documented. The arrests formed part of a wider wave of detentions ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games. Azerbaijan acknowledged the facts underlying the case in 2019, and in April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the arrests and mistreatment.

In July 2023 officers raided a private birthday party in the capital, where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of being outed.

A trans woman was murdered in the capital in March 2024 and the police investigation into the killing was inadequate. Nothing in the record indicates that the state treats the killing of a trans woman as a matter requiring serious inquiry.

No general legal protection exists against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. ILGA-Europe has ranked Azerbaijan last, 49 of 49, in Europe every year since 2015, citing a near total absence of legal protection.

Trans people cannot change their gender on official documents, although they may change their name to match their gender identity. Same-sex couples have no legal standing: marriage and civil unions are neither recognised nor performed, and same-sex couples may not adopt children.

Conscription is mandatory for able-bodied men aged 18 to 35. LGBTQIA+ enlistees can be declared unfit for service under Articles 18/b (personality disorders) and 17/b (reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders) of the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations, and queer conscripts often conceal their orientation to avoid hazing.

Hostility is also carried by official media. After a Women's Day march in the capital demanding access to trans healthcare, the state-affiliated Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people. QueeRadar monitoring found that 77% of 428 analysed media pieces were hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people, and politicians and officials have used discriminatory language to shape public perception.

Coming out carries family consequences: in 2024 a family forcibly transported an 18-year-old woman to the capital after she came out.
tangentialFactors:
Azerbaijan's constitution guarantees freedom of expression, and the Azerbaijan Press Council, founded in 2003, handles complaints under a Press Code of Conduct. A 2017 US State Department report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and the blocking of websites.

Discrimination has direct economic effects. Trans people are rejected from jobs and housing and pushed into black-market work and precarious housing; one profiled woman, 29, was arrested, denied housing and employment, and left dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer closed.

Public visibility carries risk. In July 2023 an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe.

Violence in education has produced a documented legal response. In April 2019 14-year-old Elina Hajiyeva of Baku attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at her school; the principal took no action, attributed the attempt to family difficulties and did not call an ambulance, and she died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus compensation of about $10,882. The case prompted a nationwide social media campaign, a video addressed to President Ilham Aliyev, and a Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan launched 13 May 2019 with a new hotline.

The age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. By law no groups are excluded from blood donation apart from people infected with HIV/AIDS. Critics have argued that Azerbaijan should not be allowed to host international events because of its discrimination against LGBTQIA+ people, a controversy that flared around the 2012 international song contest.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing discrimination is documented in a shadow report to the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women by the Gender & Development Social Union, which describes state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia and transphobia in official and private media, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women; the organisation serves more than 200 LBT people.

A queer-feminist platform, the Gender Resource Center (Gender Resurs Mərkəzi), was established in 2020 in response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations. Gender and Development, created in 2007, runs local projects in collaboration with the national health ministry.

LGBTQIA+ media exists despite the environment: gay.az, the first news website for LGBTQIA+ people, launched 25 May 2011, and Minority Magazine, the first LGBTQIA+ online magazine, was founded in December 2015 and became an NGO in August 2017. A documentary about a trans man premiered in Baku on 25 November 2017 with support from a Dutch embassy and drew about 80 people.

AZAD LGBT ran in-person programming in Baku, including LGBTQ movie nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-film Q&As, and launched a website in 2015 providing free online LGBTQ education tools. Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance regularly holds talks with the EU Delegation to Azerbaijan and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Azerbaijan Press Council has ever assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics is not known from the sources.

Unresolved: whether men who have sex with men are de facto permitted to donate blood, given that only HIV/AIDS infection is excluded by law, is not established.

Not sourced: whether the April 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling has been implemented, or what remedy followed the inadequate investigation into the March 2024 killing.

Not sourced: any practical procedure for changing a gender marker on Azerbaijani identity documents; the sources state only that gender cannot be changed while a name change is permitted.
